journeys.title: Faith in Public and Private
journeys.aim: Sincere belief grows into accountability, repair after mistakes, and justice without judging other hearts.

lessons.title: When No One Is Watching
story: A new year had begun at Sheikh Uncle’s Academy. This time the older students were asked to organise a “Guidance in Action” exhibition for younger pupils. The aim was not merely to display posters but to demonstrate choices they could defend.

When Akhlaq checked the equipment list, he noticed that several tablets were marked as returned although one remained in the library cupboard. It was tempting to leave the record unchanged: the team might otherwise lose permission to borrow devices for its final presentation. “We can fix it after the exhibition,” Mohsin suggested. Imaan replied, “Then the record will be inaccurate today, when someone may rely on it.”

They told Sir Zameer about the discrepancy. The teacher did not congratulate them as heroes. He asked them to trace the device, correct the form and improve their checking procedure. They found the tablet and updated the record together.

Later, Dadi Jaan asked Akhlaq why he had been so worried. “I wanted people to think our group was responsible,” he admitted. “But being responsible is not the same as appearing responsible.” Dadi nodded. “That is a useful lesson about the actions that should follow belief.” The exhibition’s first display now had an unexpected title: THE TRUE RECORD.

teaching.text: The master book teaches that Islam combines belief, worship and character. Imaan is not established by a school badge or an outward display, and an individual cannot see another person’s inner sincerity. Still, a learner can examine their own intentions and correct conduct. Qur’an 4:135 calls believers to stand firmly for justice; Sūrah al-ʿAṣr connects faith with righteous action, truth and patience. The Hadith about intentions is a reminder to ask why we do a deed, not a license to accuse classmates of hypocrisy.

Sometimes telling the truth feels uncomfortable. A responsible person neither hides mistakes to preserve a reputation nor announces someone else’s mistakes to feel superior. The right response is proportionate: identify the error, repair its consequences and prevent its repetition. Learning is measured in reliable habits and understanding, never as a public score of anyone’s Imaan.

questions.q: Does a public display prove someone’s sincerity?
questions.a: No. Allah knows hearts; people should examine their own intentions and actions.

questions.q: Why was the equipment record important?
questions.a: Other people relied on it, so accuracy was a duty.

questions.q: Does honesty always bring immediate praise?
questions.a: No. It remains right even when inconvenient.

questions.q: What should follow an admitted mistake?
questions.a: Correction, restitution where needed, and improved care.

reflect: Which duty do I handle differently when nobody is likely to notice?

scenario: Your team can hide a small error to protect its reputation. What would an honest plan look like?
decide.feedback: Check the facts, correct the report, inform the responsible adult, and take steps to avoid repeating it.

lessons.title: The Door of Return Remains Open
story: The academy had agreed that its exhibition would use recycled paper where possible. Akhlaq forgot to order supplies and, when questioned, blamed a younger volunteer. For two days he avoided the volunteer because admitting the truth felt embarrassing. By the third day, the younger pupil was being blamed in several group messages.

Imaan found Akhlaq staring at the messages. “You can correct this,” she said. “I’ve already left it too long,” he replied. “That makes it harder,” she answered, “not impossible.” Together they asked Sir Zameer to supervise the correction. Akhlaq explained the actual sequence of events, apologised to the pupil and arranged for the replacement materials.

That evening, Salaam opened the Qur’an to the verse calling people not to despair of Allah’s mercy. He explained that repentance is serious: a person should turn away from wrongdoing, regret it, intend not to repeat it, and restore other people’s rights when possible. An apology without repair may be incomplete.

Akhlaq wrote the volunteer a second note: “You deserved to be treated fairly from the beginning.” The note did not erase what happened, but it was part of a real return to responsibility. The next day he asked to manage the exhibition’s inventory under supervision.

teaching.text: Chapter 21 deals with sin, repentance and serious boundaries of belief. A learner must not conclude that every sinful action expels a Muslim from Islam. Neither should the promise of Allah’s mercy be treated as permission to wrong people deliberately. Qur’an 39:53 offers hope, while the master chapter teaches that texts about forgiveness must be understood together and in proper context. Where harm has been done to another person, sincere repentance includes taking responsible steps about their rights.

It is possible to be ashamed of a deed without believing that one has become hopeless. Some consequences persist even after a sincere apology; those injured may need time and safe boundaries. A learner does not decide whether another person’s Tawbah has been accepted by Allah. Their task is to correct their own conduct, seek help when necessary and keep choosing good actions.

questions.q: What does Tawbah mean?
questions.a: Turning back to Allah from wrongdoing.

questions.q: Can an apology replace restoring someone’s rights?
questions.a: Not when restitution or correction is possible and required.

questions.q: Should a Muslim despair after making a mistake?
questions.a: No. Seek Allah’s forgiveness and make a sincere correction.

questions.q: Can we judge whether Allah has accepted another person’s repentance?
questions.a: No. That hidden matter belongs to Allah.

reflect: When I am embarrassed, do I become more willing to blame someone else?

scenario: A student apologises for damaging a book but refuses to replace it despite being able to. What is missing?
decide.feedback: An honest apology should be joined to practical repair and respect for the other person.

lessons.title: Do Not Judge What You Cannot See
story: A short clip circulated in the class group. It showed a pupil leaving a school prayer gathering before the final discussion. Someone wrote, “He clearly does not care about religion.” By lunchtime, several others had added harsher comments. Akhlaq was about to forward the clip when Mohsina asked, “Do we know why he left?”

They learned that the pupil had been called to help his younger brother, who was unwell. Imaan asked Sir Zameer how a few seconds of video had become a judgment on someone’s heart. The teacher wrote three words on the board: EVENT, ASSUMPTION, ACCUSATION. The event was that a pupil left. The assumption was that he did not value religion. The accusation was a claim about his inner belief.

Dadi later reminded the family that Islamic teachings about faith and wrongdoing are not tools for children to use against classmates. Serious judgments have conditions, contexts and qualified scholarly procedures. The next morning the group removed the clip, apologised and agreed not to publish religious labels about anyone.
At the exhibition, Imaan offered a new activity: “What do you know, what do you assume, and what should you check?” It was one of the most visited tables.

teaching.text: The Qur’an commands verification of news and warns against suspicion and backbiting (49:6, 49:12). The master text distinguishes sins from judgments about leaving Islam and warns against unfounded Takfīr. This subject is too serious for social-media slogans or school debates. Young people can confidently learn their own religious duties while refusing to turn differences, absences or incomplete information into charges against others.

Sometimes harmful behaviour must be reported promptly even before every detail is known—for example, when a child's safety is at risk. That is different from publicly spreading allegations. A sound response separates observation from interpretation, seeks help from those responsible and protects privacy as far as safety permits. The aim is truth and justice, not winning a discussion or exposing classmates.

questions.q: What does verifying a report mean?
questions.a: Checking its source and important facts before accepting or sharing it.

questions.q: Does leaving one gathering reveal the state of a person’s heart?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Should children decide that another Muslim has left Islam?
questions.a: No. Serious judgments require expertise and proper conditions.

questions.q: What if the report concerns danger?
questions.a: Tell a trustworthy adult promptly rather than spreading gossip.

reflect: Have I ever repeated a confident judgment without knowing the whole context?

scenario: A friend asks you to share a clip with an accusation about someone’s faith. What response is responsible?
decide.feedback: Do not amplify it; check the situation and seek appropriate adult help if there is genuine concern.

journeys.title: Belief, Reason and Responsible Questions
journeys.aim: Explore questions about the Creator, science and suffering with evidence and humility.

lessons.title: The Creator Is Not a Created Thing
story: Akhlaq brought a diagram to the academy showing a chain of moving gears. “Every gear depends on another,” he said, “so who moves the first one?” Mohsin wanted to draw the Creator as the largest gear. Imaan objected: “But Allah is not a part of the machine.”

Sir Zameer agreed that diagrams can help us ask questions, but they can also mislead. The gears illustrate dependence among created things; they are not a picture of Allah. He invited the group to distinguish between a thing that needs causes and conditions and the One whom Muslims believe to be eternally independent of all creation.

Later at home, Dadi read Sūrah al-Ikhlāṣ with them. The children had memorised the verses long ago. Now they considered why the passage rejects the idea of Allah having an equal or resembling created beings.

Akhlaq revised the diagram. Instead of putting Allah inside the gear system, he wrote beneath it: “Created things depend on Allah; Allah does not depend on His creation.” The question had become clearer without pretending that a classroom drawing could capture the reality of the Divine.

teaching.text: Chapters 11 and 12 explain Allah as eternal and necessary (Wājib al-Wujūd), unlike contingent created things. The Qur’an speaks of His uniqueness and independence; it does not invite us to imagine Him as an oversized human being, object or force within nature. An illustration may show the dependency of creatures, but it cannot depict Allah’s attributes or essence.

The master manuscript introduces reasoning about why the universe and contingent existence call for explanation. At this age, the goal is to understand the distinction between a Creator and the created order, know what an argument does and does not establish, and speak with humility about matters beyond our senses. Students should not claim that every philosophical question has been solved by one analogy; careful belief and patient learning belong together.

questions.q: What does Wājib al-Wujūd mean in this lesson?
questions.a: Allah necessarily exists and depends on nothing.

questions.q: Is Allah another object inside the universe?
questions.a: No. Allah is the Creator, not part of creation.

questions.q: Can a drawing show Allah’s reality?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What can analogies help with?
questions.a: Understanding a limited idea, while remembering where the comparison fails.

reflect: When does a helpful comparison begin to mislead me?

scenario: Someone says, “Allah is like the biggest star in the universe.” How would you correct this kindly?
decide.feedback: Explain that stars are created, changing objects; Allah is not like His creation.

lessons.title: Science and Revelation Ask Different Questions
story: The academy entered a regional science fair with a project about local rainwater. Mohsina proposed testing whether two filters removed visible sediment at different rates. Akhlaq wanted to begin his poster with “Science proves every detail of my belief.” Imaan worried that such a claim would turn a practical investigation into an argument the team had not actually tested.

Their teacher asked them to identify the question the experiment could answer. “It can show which filter is more effective in our conditions,” said Mohsina. “Does it reveal all the purposes of the universe?” asked Sir Zameer. “No,” Akhlaq admitted.

They tested the samples, recorded the limitations and checked the source of their water-safety advice. When one filter performed worse than expected, they changed their conclusion instead of altering the results.

At home, Salaam encouraged the children to marvel at creation without forcing changing scientific theories into Qur’anic verses. The Qur’an encourages reflection on the world, while honest science studies testable aspects of that world. The revised poster bore two headings: WHAT WE MEASURED and WHAT WE BELIEVE. Akhlaq was relieved that he no longer had to pretend both were the same kind of statement.

teaching.text: Chapter 13 separates the question of natural mechanisms from the question of Allah as Creator. Empirical science can test observations, propose explanations and revise models. Revealed teachings address matters that include faith, worship, accountability and ultimate meaning. A philosophical argument may draw on observation, but it should not be mislabeled a laboratory result.

Students must be careful with “scientific miracle” claims that assign exact modern technical discoveries to verses without reliable exegesis. Equally, a new scientific model does not automatically settle every theological question. This is not an invitation to dismiss science; it is a call to define questions accurately and let evidence guide claims of the sort it can support. Scientific safety—particularly water and health—requires professional standards rather than theological guesses.

questions.q: What can a controlled experiment help us discover?
questions.a: A testable comparison under specified conditions.

questions.q: Should we revise an explanation after contradictory evidence?
questions.a: Yes, when the evidence warrants it.

questions.q: Is every Qur’anic verse a technical prediction?
questions.a: No. Interpret revelation with sound scholarship and context.

questions.q: Can belief encourage curiosity about creation?
questions.a: Yes, without weakening standards of scientific evidence.

reflect: Have I described a personal belief, a measured fact and an inference as though they were identical?

scenario: A friend wants to claim a Qur’anic verse proves an exact experiment before checking either one. What will you advise?
decide.feedback: Review the verse with qualified sources, describe the experiment honestly, and avoid exaggerated certainty.

lessons.title: Hardship, Qadar and Helpful Action
story: Heavy rain damaged several homes near the academy, and the older pupils organised a collection of school supplies. One volunteer said, “If the families trusted Allah, perhaps they would not need help.” Imaan stopped packing a box. “They need notebooks and safe places,” she replied. “Their difficulty is not our invitation to judge them.”

Sir Zameer asked students to separate what they could not control from their next responsible action. No child had caused the weather. They could nevertheless volunteer safely, coordinate with adults and avoid sharing affected families’ private photographs.

Akhlaq remembered their earlier lesson about Qadar and asked whether making plans contradicted reliance on Allah. Salaam answered that effort, prayer, counsel and appropriate means are part of a responsible response. The details of divine wisdom remain beyond our knowledge. A suffering person does not need simplistic explanations of why the hardship happened.

At the end of the week the pupils delivered supplies through the community centre. They did not claim to have solved every problem. On their exhibition poster, the lesson read: TRUST DOES NOT REQUIRE PASSIVITY; COMPASSION DOES NOT REQUIRE AN EXPLANATION FOR SOMEONE ELSE’S PAIN.

teaching.text: Chapter 18 teaches both Allah’s decree and the reality of accountable human choices. Chapter 20 acknowledges difficult questions about suffering. The two must not be combined into a harsh formula that blames victims. Muslims believe Allah knows and decrees events, yet human beings have duties and must use permissible means. The Qur’an reminds us that Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity (2:286), but this cannot be used to dismiss serious distress, disability or the need for professional help.

Older children can learn three separate questions: What is established by revelation? What part is uncertain to me? What useful action can I take now? In genuine emergencies adults and trained responders should lead. Reflection ought to increase mercy, not encourage students to offer unsolicited judgments about another person’s faith.

questions.q: Does belief in Qadar remove personal accountability?
questions.a: No. We remain responsible for choices within our capacity.

questions.q: Must a distressed person explain why hardship occurred?
questions.a: No. We do not know Allah’s hidden wisdom.

questions.q: Does seeking medical or practical help contradict Tawakkul?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What can a student do after a local emergency?
questions.a: Follow adult safeguarding guidance and offer appropriate practical help.

reflect: When have I been quick to explain someone’s hardship instead of helping?

scenario: A peer says a family’s illness is proof of weak belief. How could you respond?
decide.feedback: Reject the unsupported judgment, show compassion and direct practical help through trustworthy adults.

journeys.title: Revelation and the Trust of Knowledge
journeys.aim: Use the Qur’an and Sunnah with respect, context, reliable sources and care in sharing.

lessons.title: Read the Verse, Know the Context
story: The exhibition team wanted an opening quotation about justice. Mohsin found a sentence on a picture-sharing site and placed the words in quotation marks below a Qur’an icon. “Everyone shares this,” he said. Imaan asked, “Where is the sūrah and verse?”

The group searched an approved translation and found that the circulating sentence mixed a genuine religious idea with wording that was not the quoted verse. Sheikh Uncle asked them to remove the quotation marks and verify the intended passage.

Akhlaq suggested that they could simply use any translation they liked. Sir Zameer explained that translations attempt to convey meaning, while the Arabic Qur’an is the revealed text. Tafsīr adds explanation based on language, context and transmitted scholarship. A student’s personal takeaway is valuable when clearly identified, but it is not itself revelation.

The team redesigned its information cards with three different fields: QUR’ANIC REFERENCE, APPROVED MEANING and OUR PRACTICAL LESSON. They added a fourth field for questions requiring scholarly explanation.
A younger visitor asked why they had taken so long to check one quotation. Akhlaq answered, “Because the Qur’an deserves greater care than a quick internet caption.”

teaching.text: Chapters 5 and 15 teach Revelation and preservation; they also explain why understanding requires reliable explanation. We should distinguish the Uthmānī Arabic text, an English rendering of meaning, commentary and our own reflections. A translation is useful, but no translation reproduces every feature of the revealed Arabic. Context matters: an isolated phrase can be misunderstood when separated from its verse, setting or established explanation.

The Qur’an is treated as the final criterion in the master manuscript. Older children may begin citing sūrah and verse numbers, checking whether a quotation is complete, and asking teachers why exegetes explain a passage in a particular way. They should not independently derive legal rulings from a single verse or use the language of Tafsīr merely to promote their personal preference.

questions.q: What is the Qur’an in its original revealed form?
questions.a: The Arabic Revelation given to the Prophet ﷺ.

questions.q: What does Tafsīr do?
questions.a: Explains verses through recognised scholarly methods.

questions.q: Why identify a sūrah and verse?
questions.a: So readers can check wording and context.

questions.q: May a personal reflection be labeled “Allah says”?
questions.a: No. Label reflections as our understanding and keep revelation distinct.

scenario: A poster contains a beautiful sentence attributed to Qur’an but no reference. Should you publish it?
decide.feedback: Verify the Arabic and an approved rendering; if it cannot be established, remove the attribution.

lessons.title: The Sunnah Is Guidance, Not a Rumour
story: Akhlaq prepared a “Prophetic kindness” display. One card described how to speak gently; another contained an astonishing story that someone had forwarded without a reference. Both looked attractive, and the class voted that the second card was more exciting.

Before the presentation, Sheikh Uncle asked the group to identify where the story was recorded and whether a reliable scholar had evaluated it. They could not. “A good message is not permission to invent a report about the Messenger of Allah,” he explained.

They replaced the unverified story with a carefully cited teaching already used in their studies. Mohsina then suggested a real-life activity: visitors could practise giving accurate information, listening without ridicule and returning borrowed items. The display no longer depended on sensational claims.

At home, Imaan told Salamah that she once thought love for Rasulullah ﷺ meant accepting every moving account shared about him. Her mother replied, “Love also means protecting the truth about his life and trying to practise the guidance established from reliable sources.”
The team left an empty space on the display: SOURCES WE ARE STILL CHECKING. Even that empty space was an educational lesson.

teaching.text: The master text presents Muhammad ﷺ as the final Messenger and a model of character. Sunnah includes his authentic teachings, actions and approvals, while specialists apply methods to evaluate reports and their context. Not every widely circulated anecdote is a proven Hadith. Students need not become Hadith critics, but they can learn to identify references, distinguish certainty from doubt and consult qualified teachers.

The Qur’an describes the Messenger ﷺ as an excellent example (33:21). Following this example includes worship according to sound instruction, truthfulness and justice, not imitation of unverified internet legends. A hadith's moral appeal alone does not establish its chain or authenticity; historical claims must be checked before being attributed to the Prophet ﷺ.

questions.q: Why is the Sunnah important?
questions.a: It conveys authentic Prophetic guidance.

questions.q: Does a moving story automatically become a Hadith?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What should learners do with an unverified attribution?
questions.a: Do not repeat it as established; ask a knowledgeable teacher.

questions.q: How can love for the Prophet ﷺ appear in conduct?
questions.a: Through truthful learning and practising his established guidance.

reflect: Do I value exciting stories over reliable knowledge?

scenario: A group wants to post an unreferenced story as a Hadith because it promotes kindness. What should you do?
decide.feedback: Keep the good ethical message if sound, but remove the false attribution and use verified evidence.

lessons.title: Respecting the Companions, Checking Extraordinary Claims
story: A poster for the academy's history corridor contained three sections: the Ṣaḥābah, teachers who served later generations, and stories of extraordinary events. Mohsin suggested putting the most dramatic tale at the top, even though it came from an anonymous channel.

Sir Zameer asked them first to honour the Companions accurately. Their lives contained real service, sacrifices and lessons that should not be displaced by exaggerated legends. The teacher then explained that terms such as Muʿjizah and Karāmah have specific meanings in the scholarly tradition; a viral video of an unusual coincidence is not enough to establish a miracle.

Imaan rearranged the exhibition around evidence. She placed verified learning and good character first, and moved unverified stories to a notebook titled QUESTIONS FOR SCHOLARLY REVIEW. When younger pupils came, she explained the difference between respecting righteous people and worshipping them.

Akhlaq realised that an extraordinary claim could become less credible when people were too eager to believe it. “So wonder should make us careful, not careless,” he said. Sheikh Uncle replied, “That is a mature starting point.”

teaching.text: Chapter 17 honours the Ṣaḥābah and explains Awliyāʾ, Muʿjizāt and Karāmāt, while maintaining Tawḥīd. Muslims respect those whom Revelation honours; they do not treat pious people as divine or make them independent sources of worship. Extraordinary occurrences must not become proof merely because someone posts dramatic imagery or claims access to the unseen.

For this age group, students should learn useful vocabulary and why religious scholarship has rules of evidence. Disagreement about the historical authenticity of an anecdote is not disrespect toward a scholar or saint. Avoid careless dismissals, but also avoid inventing miracles or making unverified claims about the Companions. A sound teacher can help distinguish scripture, authentic report, scholarly interpretation and popular storytelling.

questions.q: Who are the Ṣaḥābah?
questions.a: The Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, according to the established scholarly definition.

questions.q: Does honouring a righteous person mean worshipping them?
questions.a: No. Worship belongs to Allah alone.

questions.q: Is a viral extraordinary video proof of a Karāmah?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What should we do with an uncertain historical tale?
questions.a: Label it uncertain and seek qualified source evaluation.

reflect: Which stories do I accept quickly because they are impressive?

journeys.title: Learning the Language of Fiqh
journeys.aim: Know what legal categories do, why scholars differ, and when a ruling requires qualified help.

lessons.title: Why Do Islamic Rulings Have Categories?
story: The exhibition team designed a board titled REQUIRED, RECOMMENDED and PERMITTED. Akhlaq placed every religiously good action in the first column, reasoning that if something was good then everyone must do it. Imaan pointed out that a person may be encouraged to perform an act without its being Fard.

They asked Sheikh Uncle to explain the terms used in their master book: Fard, Wajib, Sunnah, Mustaḥabb, Mubāḥ, Makrūh and Ḥarām. “These are not just colourful labels,” he said. “They express legal judgments reached through study of evidence. In Hanafi jurisprudence, Fard and Wajib have a technical distinction. Another school may arrange some terms differently.”

Mohsin wanted a game where pupils guessed the ruling of unfamiliar situations. Sir Zameer suggested a safer task: match clearly established examples to their definitions and place genuinely complicated cases in a box labelled ASK A QUALIFIED TEACHER.

At the final practice round, Akhlaq deliberately left one card unanswered. “There is not enough information,” he explained. His team accepted the answer. They had learned that hesitation, when justified, is part of honest knowledge.

teaching.text: Chapter 22 introduces legal classifications from the Hanafi tradition. A ruling describes the status of an action according to Islamic jurisprudence. A student should know the foundational terms, but should not conclude that similar-looking cases always share one ruling. Some obligations concern each individual; others are communal. Some acts are recommended; some are permissible, disliked or forbidden. The master text distinguishes the Hanafi usage of Wajib from Fard, so one must not collapse them into one label when summarising a Hanafi source.

A real ruling may depend on intention, circumstances, the person’s legal capacity and further evidence. Understanding that jurists reason carefully is more important than winning a quick quiz. The learner should follow a verified instructional pathway and seek trustworthy scholarly support where detailed cases arise.

questions.q: What is Fiqh?
questions.a: The juristic understanding of practical Islamic rulings from recognised evidence.

questions.q: Is every good action compulsory?
questions.a: No. Some are recommended or permissible.

questions.q: Does Hanafi Wajib always have identical usage in other schools?

lessons.title: Why Do Respected Scholars Sometimes Differ?
story: At a family visit, Akhlaq noticed that his cousin’s prayer preparation looked slightly different from the method he had learned. He whispered to Imaan, “Should I tell him that he has done it wrong?” Imaan asked him to wait until they could speak respectfully with Salaam.

The following day Sheikh Uncle gathered the older pupils around a table with four books representing the recognised Sunni schools. He explained that scholars sometimes evaluate evidence and apply legal principles differently. The team was not being asked to combine whatever option seemed easiest; they were being asked to learn why knowledgeable disagreement exists.

Mohsina read the academy’s instruction sheet. It taught the Hanafi method as the local practical pathway and marked certain comparisons for teacher-led study. Mohsin worried that recognising another school would weaken his own confidence. Sir Zameer replied that knowing the limits of personal expertise can strengthen humility, not weaken commitment.

The pupils changed the wording on their exhibition poster. Instead of “Only one method is ever taught by Muslims,” it now said, “Learn your school’s method correctly; ask respectfully about established differences.” The improved poster offered guidance without turning the prayer room into a debate hall.

teaching.text: The master curriculum uses Hanafi Fiqh as its teaching foundation and includes verified comparisons with the Mālikī, Shāfiʿī and Ḥanbalī schools when needed. These differences are not evidence that any young learner may manufacture rulings from isolated texts. Nor should one assume that every detail is disputed. Some matters are shared; others involve established differences in evidence, interpretation or classification.

Ages 13–14 can recognise this distinction and practise respectful communication. For example, school-specific approaches to Wudu or the starting time of ʿAṣr should be identified accurately, without mockery. A student ought to practise a coherent method taught by qualified people and ask about unfamiliar rulings with good manners. Comparative study aims to deepen knowledge and respect, not confuse everyday worship.

questions.q: What is a Madhhab?
questions.a: A recognised school of juristic understanding.

questions.q: Which school forms this curriculum’s practical basis?
questions.a: The Hanafi school.

questions.q: Must we mock a worshipper who follows another recognised school?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: May children freely combine isolated rulings to avoid duties?
questions.a: No. They need qualified guidance.

lessons.title: When a Short Answer Is Not a Fatwa
story: A community member asked the exhibition team whether a particular medical treatment would affect fasting. Akhlaq remembered a sentence from a lesson about accidental swallowing and almost gave an immediate answer. Mohsina stopped him: “We do not even know what treatment they mean.”

They brought the question to a teacher, who explained that medicine, route of administration, illness and the person’s circumstances can affect a real ruling. Some matters require a clinician and a qualified Hanafi scholar to work from accurate facts. The boys and girls should never be asked to publish private medical details just to demonstrate what they know.

Later another student asked whether a family business must pay Zakah on a specific investment. The team again recognised that knowing a general principle did not make them qualified accountants or jurists.

Sir Zameer praised their restraint. The revised exhibition included a flow chart: UNDERSTAND THE QUESTION → ESTABLISH THE FACTS → IDENTIFY THE RELIABLE AUTHORITY → ACT RESPONSIBLY. Imaan added, “We can explain a rule in class without issuing a ruling on a real person.”

teaching.text: The source work explains categories of obligation and numerous special cases in fasting, Zakah and prayer. However, a student chapter is not a fatwa manual. When facts vary—medical treatment, financial ownership, travel conditions, disability, puberty-related changes—an answer copied from a single paragraph may be dangerously incomplete. The Quranic instruction to refer matters to Allah and His Messenger (4:59) is not a substitute for the scholarly methods by which detailed rulings are interpreted.

A learner should be able to state the classroom principle, recognise uncertainties, protect privacy and seek relevant professional or religious advice. This is especially valuable in an era of short video clips and confident anonymous posts. Being responsible sometimes means declining to answer a personal question rather than presenting general information as an individual judgment.

journeys.title: Purity, Maturity and Compassion
journeys.aim: Apply ordinary purification with confidence while protecting privacy and health.

lessons.title: Cleanliness Without Endless Doubts
story: At the academy’s sports day, Akhlaq found a brown mark on the hem of his trousers. He began to worry that the garment might be ritually impure, even though he had no reason to think the mark was anything other than soil. After washing his hands twice, he wanted to start his entire Wudu again.

Imaan recalled their earlier lessons: ordinary dirt is not automatically Najasah, and repeated checking without evidence can create needless anxiety. They asked Salaam for help rather than making up a rule. He reviewed how one identifies a known impurity and how the ordinary Hanafi Wudu is completed.

The next day the exhibition team prepared a small teaching station with a sink, clean towels and a reminder not to waste water. Children could practise the steps calmly, without an audience counting every drop or making comments about others’ mistakes.

Akhlaq added one sentence to the poster: CAREFUL DOES NOT MEAN ENDLESS. The teacher encouraged the group to use evidence-based instruction and to obtain further help when persistent doubts make ordinary worship difficult.

teaching.text: Chapters 23–25 distinguish ordinary physical cleanliness from the ritual states relevant to Salah, and explain the Hanafi method of Wudu. The master also describes classical water classifications and well-related rules. Those historical Fiqh discussions should not be confused with modern microbiological drinking-water assessment. A clean-looking source may still be medically unsafe, while a harmless patch of soil is not automatically a ritual impurity.

At this stage, students should correctly perform ordinary Wudu, recognise when known impurity must be removed, and understand that certainty is not displaced by recurring unsupported suspicion. They should avoid excessive water use and repeated washing out of fear. Persistent distress around purification calls for sympathetic adult and qualified support, not punishment or public correction. Students do not need to memorise every technical well ruling for this lesson.

questions.a: No. The substance and legal rules matter.

questions.q: Is ordinary cleanliness identical to Wudu?
questions.a: No. Wudu is ritual purification.

questions.q: Is old well-purification Fiqh a substitute for modern drinking-water testing?
questions.a: No.

questions.a: Use the taught method calmly and seek help if doubts persist.

lessons.title: Ghusl, Growth and Personal Dignity
story: The academy planned a session on personal hygiene and growing up. Several pupils worried that classmates would be required to describe their experiences in front of everyone. Salamah, who had been invited to advise the teachers, insisted that the session should have private questions, trustworthy adults and suitable teaching arrangements.

Imaan prepared a simple explanation for younger learners about staying clean and maintaining dignity. The older learners received a carefully reviewed handout describing how Islamic law distinguishes ordinary bathing from Ghusl when a major ritual state requires it. Personal details were not collected by the group.

Akhlaq asked whether someone should be embarrassed to ask about a bodily change. Salaam replied that learning the obligations of worship is important, but a child’s privacy and wellbeing matter as well. Puberty can begin at different ages; essential instruction cannot be postponed until a particular birthday.

At the exhibition, the team displayed a modest sign: YOUR QUESTION DESERVES RESPECT. A sealed question box was managed by trained adults, not by student volunteers. No one was asked to disclose what they had experienced. The children learned that responsible education can be both clear and discreet.

teaching.text: Chapter 26 explains the Hanafi obligations of Ghusl; Chapter 28 discusses personal hygiene and modest conduct. Before or when a child reaches religious maturity, appropriate instruction must be available in language they can understand. According to the master Hanafi presentation, the obligatory Ghusl actions include rinsing the mouth, rinsing the nose and washing the whole body according to the applicable rules. Detailed cases and sex-specific matters require careful private instruction with a competent teacher.

Puberty is not a reason for shame, jokes, intrusive questions or comparisons. Children may need information earlier than classmates of the same chronological age. This unit teaches the relationship between a prescribed ritual state and correct preparation for worship while protecting dignity and offering trustworthy channels for personal questions. Medical worries should be directed to appropriate healthcare professionals; the classroom is not an intake clinic.

questions.q: Is an ordinary shower necessarily the same as a valid Ghusl?
questions.a: No. It must satisfy the applicable legal requirements.

questions.q: What is one Hanafi obligation in Ghusl?
questions.a: Rinsing the mouth, rinsing the nose or washing the whole body.

questions.q: Should children share puberty details in front of classmates?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: When should essential maturity-related teaching be available?

lessons.title: Purification When Ordinary Methods Are Difficult
story: During an outing, Mohsin hurt his ankle and arrived at the academy with a medical dressing. Some students suggested that he remove it whenever he made Wudu. Mohsina objected: “His clinician told him not to disturb the dressing. We should not give risky instructions.”

The team consulted a qualified adult, who explained that Islamic jurisprudence includes rules for dressings, wiping and situations where ordinary washing is harmful. They discussed Tayammum as a prescribed alternative in specific circumstances, not an excuse to avoid safe water whenever it feels inconvenient.

Akhlaq remembered a classmate who had limited mobility and needed more time at the washing area. He persuaded the exhibition planners to allow accessible paths and enough space for assistance. The teacher reminded them that helping with access was part of making religious learning practical.

The students’ display did not ask visitors to perform a mock wounded-person challenge. Instead, it invited them to choose respectful responses: move equipment, provide privacy, ask before helping and seek qualified religious and medical advice. The most important lesson was that concessions express Allah’s mercy, not another person’s failure.

teaching.text: The master explains Masah over suitable footwear and dressings in Chapter 27, Tayammum in Chapter 29 and prayer during illness in Chapter 37. Each has legal conditions that matter. A student cannot infer the proper method for every wound, cast, clinical restriction or water shortage from a short summary. In the established Hanafi method, legal classification, duration and actual ability are relevant to cases involving Masah and Tayammum.

For ages 13–14 the educational outcome is recognising the presence of genuine concessions and knowing how to obtain accurate guidance. Medical professionals assess harm; qualified religious teachers explain the applicable worship rules. Disability should never be portrayed as a defect in faith, and learners must not be pressured to perform an unsafe action to satisfy a generic classroom demonstration.

questions.a: No. It has specified legal conditions.

questions.a: No.

journeys.aim: Strengthen correct prayer, understand repair, and recognise lawful concessions.

lessons.title: Prepared Before the Opening Takbīr
story: The academy exhibition was opening in ten minutes, and the team still needed to pray. Akhlaq grabbed a prayer mat and hurried towards the nearest room. Imaan stopped him long enough to ask whether the prayer time had entered and the room was suitable.

They reviewed the seven conditions taught in the original curriculum: purity of body, clothes and place; the appropriate covering; correct time; Qiblah; and intention. Sir Zameer made clear that these are prerequisites before Salah, not seven extra movements inside each Rakʿah.

After verifying the prayer space and timetable once, they began calmly. Mohsin had wanted to hurry through the prayer to finish the exhibits. Afterwards, he said that careful preparation had actually reduced his anxiety about being late.

The team then placed a helpful poster by the prayer area. Its tone was neither threatening nor childish: PREPARE CORRECTLY, THEN WORSHIP WITH ATTENTION. Alongside the poster was a practical sign showing where to leave shoes, how to maintain clear walkways and whom to ask if a person needed assistance.

teaching.text: Chapters 9, 30 and 32 develop the sequence and legal structure of Salah. The master lists seven conditions before Salah and distinguishes them from the internal Fard actions and Wajib duties. Learners should be able to name and apply the prerequisites, understand that Niyyah is fundamentally an intention of the heart, and treat worship with attentiveness.

Correctness matters, but a student should not become trapped in endless checks of the Qiblah, clothing or imagined impurities. A reasonable check through reliable means is ordinarily enough for educational practice. The master also introduces recognised school differences in prayer times and details; older students should learn their coherent Hanafi practice without shaming others. Prayer instruction and Arabic recitation must be verified and taught by competent adults.

questions.a: Examples: ritual purity, covering, prayer time, Qiblah or intention.

questions.q: Is Niyyah fundamentally a spoken formula?
questions.a: No. It is the intention in the heart.

questions.q: Should every prayer begin with repeated anxious rechecking?
questions.a: No. Prepare reasonably and act on reliable knowledge.

scenario: Your group wants to pray immediately without checking the time. What is the wise next step?

lessons.title: Correcting a Prayer Mistake Without Panic
story: During a practice lesson, Akhlaq realised that he did not remember which prayer mistakes required Sajdah Sahw and which required a different correction. His first idea was to create a single rule: “If anything goes wrong, repeat the whole prayer.”

Sir Zameer explained that the classical Hanafi teaching distinguishes Fard requirements, Wajib duties, Sunnah practices, Makrūh acts and invalidators. The correct response depends on what actually happened and sometimes on further conditions. A broad rule that always orders repetition is neither accurate nor kind.

The students prepared a learning board with three boxes: IDENTIFY THE ISSUE, CONSULT THE VERIFIED RULE, and SEEK QUALIFIED HELP FOR SPECIAL CASES. They used clearly fictional examples and did not ask anyone to disclose errors from their actual prayers.

At home, Akhlaq practised remembering the names of the categories without turning every moment of uncertainty into a new problem. “I thought knowing more rulings would make me anxious,” he told Salaam. His father replied, “Accurate knowledge should help you worship with confidence. When a genuine question arises, learn its correct answer rather than inventing a penalty.”

teaching.text: Chapter 35 teaches that prayer mistakes do not all carry the same legal consequence. Its Hanafi discussion includes Mufsidaat (invalidators), Makroohaat (disapproved acts) and Sajdah Sahw (a prescribed correction for certain omissions or mistakes). Students should understand these classifications and know that the method of correction is not interchangeable across cases.

This book cannot safely provide a universal diagnostic algorithm for every possible mistake. A practical demonstration of Sajdah Sahw should come from a verified Hanafi teaching guide with exact conditions and method; serious recurrent doubt also requires calm, qualified guidance. Shame-based feedback—“your worship is worthless”—must never be used. Our goal is precise learning followed by proportionate correction.

questions.q: Are all prayer mistakes legally identical?
questions.a: No. Different categories lead to different rulings.

questions.q: What is Sajdah Sahw?
questions.a: A prescribed corrective prostration for specified prayer errors.

questions.q: Should every forgotten Sunnah automatically trigger repetition?
questions.a: No.

lessons.title: Following the Imam, Travelling and Falling Ill
story: On a weekend trip, the academy group stopped at a prayer facility. The congregation had already begun. Mohsin rushed towards the front, nearly bumping into a worshipper using a walking aid. Imaan signalled to him to slow down and join calmly.

Later the children asked about the legal terms they had heard: Imām, Muqtadī, Masbūq and Musāfir. Their teacher explained that how a latecomer completes prayer depends on recognised rules, and that travel may bring concessions under specified conditions. Students should not simply assume every journey qualifies in the same way.

An older visitor also asked where someone who was unable to stand might pray. The group made space and offered assistance only after asking. Sir Zameer reminded them that Islamic law has guided methods for illness, but the classroom summary was not a substitute for personal advice.

Back at school they added a practical visitor guide: ARRIVE CALMLY; FOLLOW THE IMAM; RESPECT ACCESS NEEDS; ASK ABOUT SPECIAL CONDITIONS. Akhlaq wrote the final line himself: “Learning the congregation is also learning how not to disturb other worshippers.”

teaching.text: The master Chapters 36 and 37 explain congregational prayer, latecomers, leadership, illness and travel. Chapter 38 introduces other significant congregations. Older learners should understand the importance of not racing the Imam, arriving without harming others, and following a valid method when late. Hanafi rules for travel and shortened prayer have specific conditions, and prayer during illness has its own well-developed concessions.

Learning these concepts should increase independence but not encourage students to improvise personal rules about mobility, disability or medical treatment. Students should know the relevant terms and their basic meanings, use appropriately qualified guidance in live cases, and treat worshippers with patience. The fact that someone prays differently because of a concession is not evidence of spiritual inferiority.

questions.q: What is a Masbūq?

journeys.title: Ramadan, Discipline and Mercy
journeys.aim: Join fasting with character, careful distinctions and sincere commitments.

lessons.title: Fasting Changes More Than a Timetable
story: The academy planned a Ramadan project called A WEEK OF USEFUL DEEDS. At first Akhlaq suggested a public list showing who had fasted the most days. Imaan objected that a classmate might be ill, travelling or not yet legally obliged to fast. Besides, a leaderboard could not measure sincerity.

The team changed the project to focus on respectful behaviour: returning borrowed things, keeping promises, giving someone time to speak and helping prepare a shared meal without waste. Sir Zameer explained that fasting is a prescribed form of worship with conditions, but its ethical lessons include discipline and avoiding harmful speech.

During a long afternoon, Mohsin became irritable and snapped at a younger child. He apologised later, explaining that tiredness was not permission to be cruel. The group practised planning difficult tasks, resting appropriately and treating others with patience.

At the evening gathering, Dadi Jaan reminded them that Ramadan is a month of Qur’an, worship and care. The children agreed to keep a private reflection notebook instead of collecting one another’s fasting records. The exhibition’s Ramadan display now asked: WHAT DOES WORSHIP CHANGE IN THE WAY WE TREAT PEOPLE?

teaching.text: Chapter 39 explains the duty of fasting Ramadan for those legally obliged and able, alongside the intention, prescribed times and ethical dimension of Sawm. Chapter 34 introduces Taraweeh and Qur’anic worship during the month. Fasting is not simply a challenge of hunger or thirst; the Qur’an connects it to Taqwā (2:183), and authentic teachings call for guarding speech and behaviour.

Children aged 13–14 may have different legal responsibilities depending on maturity and circumstances, so public comparisons are not appropriate. Students should learn the general method of fasting while knowing that illness, disability and other lawful exemptions require qualified support. A child must never be pressed to fast unsafely to gain a classroom reward. Reflection should focus on gratitude, self-control and compassion, not a competition over private worship.

questions.a: Developing Taqwā, or God-consciousness.

questions.q: Is a fast just the experience of hunger?
questions.a: No. It is prescribed worship joined to good conduct.

questions.q: Should schools rank children by fasting days?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Are some people entitled to lawful exemptions?
questions.a: Yes, under established conditions.

lessons.title: When a Fast Is Interrupted
story: A video circulated before Ramadan claiming that every accidental sip of water made a fast invalid and required a severe penalty. Akhlaq began writing the statement on an information card. Imaan remembered that the class had studied authentic guidance about a person who eats or drinks forgetfully during a fast.

They checked the master chapter and discovered that it treats several different categories: forgetfulness, actions that invalidate a fast, Qadāʾ, Kaffārah, Fidyah and recognised excuses. The details could not be responsibly reduced to one sweeping caption.

Mohsina suggested an exhibit showing the difference between a general rule and a personal case. Instead of asking visitors about their own fasting, the students used anonymous fictional questions and identified which facts were needed before qualified advice could be given.

A younger student asked what should happen if someone becomes ill. Sir Zameer explained that medical safety comes first and that the relevant Fiqh ruling depends on the person's circumstances; a qualified scholar should guide the application. The team removed the frightening video caption and replaced it with a calmer instruction: LEARN THE DISTINCTIONS; ASK FOR HELP WHEN NEEDED.

teaching.text: Chapter 40 is detailed because fasting cases can differ in significant ways. The master distinguishes forgetful eating from certain accidental or intentional acts and explains Qadāʾ, Kaffārah and Fidyah in the Hanafi tradition. It also warns against mechanically applying historical quantities or contemporary medical examples without specialist review.

For older learners, the educational objective is understanding that the categories are not interchangeable. A rule about a deliberate violation does not necessarily apply to forgetfulness or a legitimate medical reason. Personal cases involving pregnancy, menstruation, chronic illness or medication should never become classroom guessing games. In real situations, a competent clinician and qualified religious scholar may both be needed. This age-level lesson intentionally does not issue individual penalties.

questions.q: Does forgetfulness always have the same ruling as deliberate eating?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: What is Qadāʾ?
questions.a: A required replacement fast in circumstances defined by law.

questions.q: Are Kaffārah and Fidyah identical?
questions.a: No; their causes and applications differ.

questions.q: Should peers decide private medical fasting cases?
questions.a: No.

lessons.title: Quiet Worship and Keeping Promises
story: Akhlaq wanted to challenge his friends to spend an entire weekend without talking, using phones or leaving a school room. He called the idea “our own Iʿtikāf.” Sheikh Uncle gently explained that Iʿtikāf is a defined form of worship with legal conditions; an ordinary school quiet-time challenge is not automatically the prescribed retreat.

Imaan suggested a safer educational activity: choose a short time to read, reflect and reduce distractions without claiming to have completed a formal rite. Mohsina designed a checklist of kind actions to do before and after the quiet session.

Later one student promised aloud, “If I get the best marks, I will never eat sweets again.” The group laughed, but Dadi Jaan asked them to consider why Islam treats vows as serious commitments rather than casual bargains. Not every spontaneous remark is a binding vow, and the consequences of particular wording require qualified guidance.

By the exhibition day, the pupils had replaced the extreme challenge with a thoughtful station called TIME WITH PURPOSE. It encouraged deliberate worship, honest promises and consultation with a knowledgeable adult before making unusual religious commitments.

teaching.text: Chapter 41 distinguishes types of Iʿtikāf, its basic conditions, and the rulings of devotional vows. These are structured legal topics, not merely exercises in staying silent or enduring discomfort. Students may learn the benefits of solitude for worship and the importance of avoiding distractions, but should not pretend a casual activity has the status of a prescribed ritual.

A vow or oath may have binding consequences depending on its exact terms and circumstances. Adolescents should avoid using religious promises as incentives, threats or displays of intensity. They may make practical personal plans—such as setting aside reading time—without turning every plan into a vow to Allah. Teacher guidance should recognise different needs and provide safe alternatives for students who cannot participate in certain activities.

journeys.title: Wealth, Rights and Responsible Service
journeys.aim: Learn why giving is an act of worship and how financial ethics protect dignity.

lessons.title: Zakah Is a Right, Not a Trophy
story: The academy planned to collect school bags for families who needed them. Akhlaq wanted to publish a list of families alongside the names of donors so everybody could see who had helped. Mohsina pointed out that the project belonged to the people receiving the supplies as much as to those giving them. “Why should someone’s need become our advertisement?” she asked.

Salaam explained that Zakah is not simply a trophy for generosity; it is a duty on qualifying wealth with defined conditions and recipients. The team’s collection was voluntary charity, not automatically a substitute for anyone’s personal Zakah calculation.

The students changed their plan. Adults verified what families actually needed, arranged distribution discreetly and kept private records only where necessary for accountability. No child was asked to disclose household income or whether parents had paid Zakah.

At the end, Imaan told visitors that respecting the recipient mattered as much as the number of donated items. The project’s final poster read: GIVE WITH JUSTICE, RECORD WITH CARE, PROTECT DIGNITY. Akhlaq crossed the public donor ranking off his original plan.

teaching.text: Chapter 42 teaches Zakah as a form of worship tied to qualifying ownership, Nisāb, the relevant passage of time where applicable, eligible recipients and other conditions. It also teaches Ṣadaqat al-Fiṭr separately and explains that contemporary financial products need specialist review. An adolescent can understand the ethical principles without calculating a real family’s obligation or assuming that every charitable payment automatically discharges Zakah.

The Qur’an identifies categories of Zakah recipients (9:60). Our classroom goal is to learn that giving protects rights and dignity, and that financial obligations should be handled accurately and discreetly. A learner may practise keeping fictional records and applying a simple, clearly hypothetical one-fortieth illustration where appropriate, while real calculations remain the responsibility of competent adults and qualified jurists.

questions.q: Can every charity project automatically count as Zakah?

questions.q: Where are the categories of Zakah recipients identified?

questions.q: Should learners disclose household income?

lessons.title: Money, Trust and Careful Numbers
story: The charity committee received donations of notebooks and pencils, but its inventory sheet mixed boxes of ten with individual items. On paper, the total looked far higher than the actual number. Akhlaq was tempted to publish the impressive number and correct it privately after delivery.

Imaan asked the committee to count the items again and display only verified totals. The team discovered that one row had been entered twice. They corrected it and arranged fair distribution according to the agreed needs.

In a separate exercise, Salaam showed the children a fictional amount of savings and asked what one-fortieth would be in simple arithmetic. He made clear that this was a maths exercise, not a complete Zakah assessment. The rules concerning ownership, date, eligible property and modern investments required much more than a multiplication problem.

Mohsin helped create a sample record with three columns: amount received, amount distributed and amount remaining. At the exhibition visitors were invited to find the error in a fictional ledger. The lesson was not financial cleverness for its own sake; it was the trust involved when other people depend on your numbers.

teaching.text: The master Chapter 42 emphasises lawful financial responsibility and the requirements of Zakah. For adolescents, understanding an elementary percentage or fraction is helpful, but the juristic status of specific financial assets cannot be decided from arithmetic alone. The Hanafi discussion of jewelry, qualifying property, debts and ownership must be represented accurately and checked where modern products are involved.

The character lesson is equally important: falsified totals, misleading figures and public pressure on recipients undermine the purpose of giving. Charity projects can teach accountability if adults handle personal data, consent and distribution respectfully. A transparent record is not the same as exposing a needy family’s circumstances. Privacy and honest reporting can coexist.

questions.q: Why does record accuracy matter in charity?
questions.a: Because donations are entrusted for others’ benefit.

questions.q: Does a one-fortieth calculation by itself settle Zakah?
questions.a: No. Legal eligibility and conditions must be established.

questions.q: Should an inaccurate total be left in a public report?
questions.a: No.

questions.q: Can donor accountability coexist with recipient privacy?

lessons.title: Service Without Status
story: As the exhibition drew near, the student committee disagreed about who should stand at the entrance and who should clean the tables afterward. Akhlaq wanted the most visible position. Mohsin said he had done the difficult logistics and deserved to be recognised. Meanwhile, the accessibility signs had not yet been installed.

Dadi Jaan visited during preparation and asked them who was being left out of the conversation. Imaan noticed that several younger pupils would arrive with relatives who needed step-free access. The committee reorganised the duties: one team improved directions, another managed registration, and a third cleaned and checked the rooms after visitors departed.
When the day finished, there were no awards for most visible volunteer. The chair team had worked just as hard as the speakers, and the children thanked the building staff.

Akhlaq wrote in his notebook that religious education had repeatedly returned to the same point: worship should make people more trustworthy, not more eager to appear important. On the final noticeboard, he wrote a question to take home: WHOM DID OUR WORK ACTUALLY HELP?

teaching.text: The master book begins with Islam as a way of belief, worship and character, and returns to rights and generosity in Chapter 42. Qur’an 16:90 commands justice and good conduct. Children should therefore see community service as more than a ceremonial photo or a public display of piety. A service project ought to meet genuine needs with proper consent, safe supervision and respect for the people involved.

Social status, family wealth and popularity are not measures of moral worth. Students may reflect on their own motives, share credit fairly and fulfil behind-the-scenes duties. This does not erase the importance of prescribed worship; kind conduct and ritual obligations are complementary responsibilities. Privacy, accessibility and accurate records make service more meaningful for everyone.

journeys.title: Pilgrimage and the Life We Carry Home
journeys.aim: See Hajj and Umrah as ordered worship linked to patience, justice and lifelong conduct.

lessons.title: The Hajj Begins With a Prepared Heart
story: For the exhibition’s final learning journey, Akhlaq prepared a large map of Makkah. He wanted to show how fast a pilgrim could complete each stop. Imaan asked whether speed was truly the most important measure of the journey.

Salaam explained that Hajj is an obligation for those who meet its conditions, including genuine ability, and that pilgrimage is not a race or a tourist challenge. The children read the Qur’anic guidance to avoid wrongdoing and quarrelling during Hajj.

Mohsina suggested that the map include reminders about people who might move slowly, need assistance or have different circumstances. They added a note that routes, permits and real-time arrangements belong to the official authorities and qualified guides, not to a school chart.

During the school exhibition, a visitor asked how someone could practise Hajj’s ethical lessons before being old enough or able to travel. Akhlaq now had an answer: learn patience in a queue, do not push for attention, keep promises and use shared spaces respectfully. The map became less about rushing between landmarks and more about preparing the heart for worship.

teaching.text: Chapter 43 explains the fifth pillar, its obligation upon those who have legal capacity and the central principles of the rites. The master draws on Qur’an 3:97 and 2:196–197, and teaches that worship must not be separated from ethical behaviour. The exact requirements of ability, personal health, finances and travel are not decided by a student textbook.

The educational task is to distinguish the obligation itself from a child’s aspiration, to recognise the sanctity of pilgrimage and to practise patience and service. A pilgrim needs official instructions and specialised Fiqh guidance, and travel arrangements change. The serious ethical teaching about avoiding indecency, sin and quarrelling should be retained in an age-appropriate manner without turning adult-specific legal details into a game.

lessons.title: Learning the Hajj Sequence Without Losing Its Meaning
story: The team created a floor-length Hajj timeline with five dates. Akhlaq placed the ninth of Dhul-Ḥijjah before the eighth, then moved Muzdalifah into the wrong position. He laughed and said, “At least the names are all there.” Sheikh Uncle reminded him that Hajj’s prescribed acts and order matter, even when a chart is only for learning.

They checked the ordinary educational example of Tamattuʿ used in the master text: the pilgrim has completed Umrah and later enters a new Ihram for Hajj, proceeds to Mina, stands at ʿArafāt on the appointed day, then moves to Muzdalifah after sunset and continues the prescribed rites. Some earlier steps differ for Ifrād and Qirān.

The team revised the map using dates, places and short descriptions. They avoided assigning exact modern travel hours or crowd routes because actual arrangements depend on the year and official direction.

At the exhibition, a younger learner asked why the order had to be learned so carefully. Imaan replied, “Because worship has an appointed form. Understanding the reason for care can help us approach it with respect, not as a sequence of tourist attractions.”

teaching.text: Chapter 44 is an expanded educational synthesis not provided as a complete itinerary in the original English Taʿleem-ul-Islam. It teaches the ordinary Tamattuʿ route while noting different features of Ifrād and Qirān. Hajj rituals have legal distinctions among conditions, pillars, Wajib acts and other practices; a learner cannot simply rearrange them.

For ages 13–14, a chronological map is useful, but it should remain a learning tool. Students may name Mina, ʿArafāt, Muzdalifah and the important days, identify that Wuquf at ʿArafāt has a central status, and know that actual pilgrims require authorised guides and individual advice for omissions, menstruation, illness, disability, proxies and penalties. The Qur’anic injunction to practise patience and refrain from quarrelling remains central to every learning activity.

lessons.title: Umrah Ends, Responsibility Continues
story: The exhibition was ready to close. Akhlaq stood by the final display showing four parts of Umrah: entering Ihram at the relevant point, Tawaf, Saʿi and the legally required completion through hair removal or shortening. A younger visitor confused Saʿi with Tawaf, so Imaan used two simple diagram cards to show the difference without pretending that the classroom activity performed an actual rite.

Someone asked whether touching the Black Stone was necessary even if it meant pushing other people. Mohsina reminded the visitors that a recommended practice never licenses harm. The group also explained that Umrah and Hajj are distinct acts with different prescribed rites.

At the closing family gathering, Sheikh Uncle asked what each learner would carry away from all four books. Mohsin chose checking information; Imaan chose patient attention in worship; Akhlaq chose correcting mistakes without shame. Salamah reminded them that knowledge is not complete merely because a volume ends.

The children rolled up the maps and returned the exhibition books to the library. On the final card Akhlaq wrote: GUIDANCE CONTINUES AFTER THE LAST PAGE. The team agreed to revisit its lessons through daily practice, thoughtful questions and service.

teaching.text: The master Chapter 45 is a newly authored Umrah expansion. It presents the sequence with the Hanafi distinction between Ihram as an essential condition, Tawaf as the central Fard, and Saʿi and hair removal as Wajib in its framework, while noting differing classifications among recognised schools. Students should understand the order and what the rites mean without pretending that an illustrated game substitutes for worship.

An actual pilgrim must seek qualified instruction about the Miqat, special circumstances and any missed rite, as well as current official requirements. Ethical learning continues after the journey: one should not neglect other people’s rights, use worship as a badge of superiority, or behave harshly around crowded sacred places. This final lesson links pilgrimage to the wider themes of Imaan, correct practice, mercy and responsible action.
